claim: Mice with a dysfunctional FN-synergy motif (Fn1syn/syn) suffer from mild platelet adhesion and bleeding defects due to delayed thrombus formation after vessel injury.
source: We report that mice with a dysfunctional FN-synergy motif (Fn1syn/syn) suffer from surprisingly mild platelet adhesion and bleeding defects due to delayed thrombus formation after vessel injury.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including bleeding time measurements and thrombus formation assays.

claim: Additional loss of β3 integrins in Fn1syn/syn mice dramatically aggravates the bleedings and severely compromises smooth muscle cell coverage of the vasculature leading to embryonic lethality.
source: Additional loss of β3 integrins dramatically aggravates the bleedings and severely compromises smooth muscle cell coverage of the vasculature leading to embryonic lethality.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by data from compound mutant mice showing embryonic lethality and vascular defects.

claim: The synergy site is dispensable for the initial contact of α5β1 with the RGD motif.
source: Cell-based studies revealed that the synergy site is dispensable for the initial contact of α5β1 with the RGD, but essential to re-enforce the binding of α5β1/αIIbβ3 to FN.
evidence: The abstract states this conclusion, which is supported by cell adhesion assays and single-cell force spectroscopy experiments showing no difference in initial binding rates.

claim: The synergy site is essential to re-enforce the binding of α5β1/αIIbβ3 to FN.
source: Cell-based studies revealed that the synergy site is dispensable for the initial contact of α5β1 with the RGD, but essential to re-enforce the binding of α5β1/αIIbβ3 to FN.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by spinning disk assays, crosslinking experiments, and platelet adhesion studies under flow.

claim: The FN synergy site is critical when external forces exceed a certain threshold or when αvβ3 integrin levels decrease below a critical level.
source: Our findings demonstrate a critical role for the FN synergy site when external forces exceed a certain threshold or when αvβ3 integrin levels decrease below a critical level.
evidence: The abstract states this conclusion, which is supported by experiments showing defects under shear flow and in β3 integrin-deficient contexts.

claim: FN is essential for mammalian development and tissue regeneration.
source: FN is essential for mammalian development and tissue regeneration, and can influence disease such as cancer progression.
evidence: This statement in the introduction is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations to prior work.

claim: The major cell-binding site in FN is an arginine-glycine-aspartate (RGD) motif located in the 10th type III module (FNIII10) that is recognized by α5β1, αIIbβ3, and αv-class integrins.
source: The major cell-binding site in FN is an arginine-glycine-aspartate (RGD) motif located in the 10th type III module (FNIII10) that is recognized by α5β1, αIIbβ3, and αv-class integrins.
evidence: This statement is based on established scientific knowledge about fibronectin structure and integrin binding.

claim: The FN synergy site in the FNIII9 module binds α5β1 and αIIbβ3 integrins but not αv-class integrins.
source: In addition to the RGD motif, FN harbors the so-called FN synergy site in the FNIII9 module (Obara et al., 1988), which binds α5β1 and αIIbβ3 integrins but not αv-class integrins (Bowditch et al., 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work (Obara et al., 1988; Bowditch et al., 1994).

claim: The synergy site encompasses the DRVPPSRN sequence in mouse FN.
source: The synergy site encompasses the DRVPPSRN sequence in mouse FN and site directed mutagenesis identified the two arginine residues to be essential for all synergy site-induced functions (Aota et al., 1994; Friedland et al., 2009; Chada et al., 2006; Nagae et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work on mutagenesis studies.

claim: The two arginine residues in the synergy site are essential for all synergy site-induced functions.
source: The synergy site encompasses the DRVPPSRN sequence in mouse FN and site directed mutagenesis identified the two arginine residues to be essential for all synergy site-induced functions (Aota et al., 1994; Friedland et al., 2009; Chada et al., 2006; Nagae et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior mutagenesis studies.

claim: The synergy site increases cell spreading in vitro.
source: In vitro studies have shown that the synergy site increases cell spreading (Aota et al., 1991), FN fibril assembly (Sechler et al., 1997) and platelet adhesion to FN (Chada et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior in vitro studies (Aota et al., 1991).

claim: The synergy site increases FN fibril assembly in vitro.
source: In vitro studies have shown that the synergy site increases cell spreading (Aota et al., 1991), FN fibril assembly (Sechler et al., 1997) and platelet adhesion to FN (Chada et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior in vitro studies (Sechler et al., 1997).

claim: The synergy site increases platelet adhesion to FN in vitro.
source: In vitro studies have shown that the synergy site increases cell spreading (Aota et al., 1991), FN fibril assembly (Sechler et al., 1997) and platelet adhesion to FN (Chada et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior in vitro studies (Chada et al., 2006).

claim: The RGD motif forms a flexible loop that physically interacts with both the α5 and β1 integrin subunits.
source: Based on the crystal structures, the RGD motif forms a flexible loop that physically interacts with both the α5 and β1 integrin subunits, while the synergy site contacts only the head domain of the α subunit (Redick et al., 2000; Nagae et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is based on crystal structure studies cited in the text (Redick et al., 2000; Nagae et al., 2012).

claim: The synergy site contacts only the head domain of the α subunit of integrins.
source: Based on the crystal structures, the RGD motif forms a flexible loop that physically interacts with both the α5 and β1 integrin subunits, while the synergy site contacts only the head domain of the α subunit (Redick et al., 2000; Nagae et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is based on crystal structure studies cited in the text (Redick et al., 2000; Nagae et al., 2012).

claim: Fn1syn/syn mice are viable and fertile.
source: Intercrossing of heterozygous mice (Fn1+/syn), which showed no apparent phenotype, gave rise to homozygous offspring (Fn1syn/syn) with a normal Mendelian ratio before and after weaning. Fn1syn/syn mice were fertile, had normal size and weight, and aged normally.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by breeding data.

claim: Fn1syn/syn mice have normal organ morphology and ultrastructure.
source: The morphology, ultrastructure, and FN distribution in heart (Figure 1B), liver, kidney, and lung (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) were indistinguishable between Fn1syn/syn and control littermates.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by histological images in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Blood vessel organization is normal in Fn1syn/syn mice.
source: Blood vessel organization in whole mount ear samples analyzed by anti-PECAM-1 and anti-αSMA immunostainings revealed no abnormalities (Figure 1C), and the subendothelial matrix visualized with antibodies to laminin-1, collagen IV and FN, was also normally organized in Fn1syn/syn mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunostaining images in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The FN synergy site is dispensable for development and postnatal homeostasis.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that the FN synergy site is dispensable for development and postnatal homeostasis.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the normal development and organ structure observed in Fn1syn/syn mice.

claim: Fn1syn/syn mice have significantly prolonged bleeding time compared to wild-type mice (7.27 ± 1.71 min vs 4.64 ± 1.50 min).
source: We measured tail bleeding time after tail biopsy (Figure 1D) and found a significant increase from 4.64 ± 1.50 min (mean ± SD) in Fn1+/+ mice to 7.27 ± 1.71 min in Fn1syn/syn mice (p<0.001).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numerical values and statistical significance, and supported by data in Figure 1D.

claim: Blood platelet counts are normal in Fn1syn/syn mice.
source: Importantly, blood platelet counts were normal in Fn1syn/syn mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: The FN content in platelets from Fn1syn/syn mice is significantly reduced to 70% compared to wild-type.
source: Since αIIbβ3 integrins mediate the uptake of pFN into platelet α-granules (Ni et al., 2003a), we performed Western-blotting with lysates from washed platelets and found that the FN content was significantly reduced to 70% in platelets from Fn1syn/syn mice (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is stated in the text with a specific percentage and supported by Western blot data in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Plasma FN levels are similar in Fn1+/+ (318.7 ± 24.1 μg/ml) and Fn1syn/syn (316.1 ± 31.0 μg/ml) mice.
source: while the levels of pFN were similar in Fn1+/+ (318.7 ± 24.1 μg/ml) and Fn1syn/syn (316.1 ± 31.0 μg/ml) mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numerical values and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Plasma fibrinogen levels are similar in Fn1+/+ (2.10 ± 0.17 mg/ml) and Fn1syn/syn (2.08 ± 0.07 mg/ml) mice.
source: Importantly, plasma levels of fibrinogen were also similar in Fn1+/+ (2.10 ± 0.17 mg/ml) and Fn1syn/syn (2.08 ± 0.07 mg/ml) mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numerical values.

claim: In vitro aggregation of washed platelets induced with collagen I, thrombin or ADP triggers normal shape changes and aggregations in Fn1syn/syn mice.
source: In vitro aggregation of washed platelets, induced with either collagen I, thrombin or ADP, triggered normal shape changes and aggregations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by aggregation assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–E.

claim: The time required for arteriole occlusion is significantly increased in Fn1syn/syn mice (28.56 ± 10.24 min) compared to Fn1+/+ mice (17.82 ± 9.74 min).
source: In contrast, the time required for arteriole occlusion was significantly increased in Fn1syn/syn mice (28.56 ± 10.24 min) compared to Fn1+/+ mice (17.82 ± 9.74 min) (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numerical values and supported by data in Figure 1G.

claim: In 3 out of 11 Fn1syn/syn mice, no total occlusion was observed after 40 min in the arteriole injury assay.
source: Notably, in 3 out of 11 Fn1syn/syn mice no total occlusion was observed after 40 min (Figure 1H), a defect that was never observed in control mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numbers and supported by data in Figure 1H.

claim: The synergy site is required to stabilize platelet clots in vivo and to prevent prolonged bleeding times.
source: These results demonstrate that the synergy site is dispensable for development and postnatal homeostasis but is required to stabilize platelet clots in vivo and to prevent prolonged bleeding times.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the bleeding time and thrombus formation data.

claim: Fn1-KO cells assemble fibrillar FN networks of indistinguishable complexity, fibril diameter and length with plasma from Fn1syn/syn and Fn1+/+ mice.
source: In line with our immunostaining of FN in tissues from Fn1syn/syn mice, Fn1-KO cells assembled fibrillar FN networks of indistinguishable complexity, fibril diameter and length with plasma from Fn1syn/syn and Fn1+/+ mice, respectively (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence images in Figure 2A.

claim: The formation of nascent adhesions (NAs) is similar on pFNwt and pFNsyn.
source: While the formation of nascent adhesions (NAs) was similar on pFNwt and pFNsyn (Figure 2B), the numbers as well as percentage of paxillin-positive focal adhesions (FAs) linked to stress fibers were significantly reduced in Fn1-KO fibroblasts seeded for 30 min on pFNsyn (Figure 2D,E)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2B.

claim: The numbers and percentage of paxillin-positive focal adhesions (FAs) linked to stress fibers are significantly reduced in Fn1-KO fibroblasts seeded for 30 min on pFNsyn.
source: While the formation of nascent adhesions (NAs) was similar on pFNwt and pFNsyn (Figure 2B), the numbers as well as percentage of paxillin-positive focal adhesions (FAs) linked to stress fibers were significantly reduced in Fn1-KO fibroblasts seeded for 30 min on pFNsyn (Figure 2D,E)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by quantification data in Figure 2D,E.

claim: The transition from NAs to mature, stress fiber-anchored FAs is delayed on pFNsyn.
source: While the formation of nascent adhesions (NAs) was similar on pFNwt and pFNsyn (Figure 2B), the numbers as well as percentage of paxillin-positive focal adhesions (FAs) linked to stress fibers were significantly reduced in Fn1-KO fibroblasts seeded for 30 min on pFNsyn (Figure 2D,E) indicating that the transition from NAs to mature, stress fiber-anchored FAs is delayed on pFNsyn.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the focal adhesion quantification data.

claim: Cell spreading is delayed in the first 30 min on pFNsyn-coated substrates.
source: Furthermore, cell spreading determined as cell area at different time points after cell seeding onto pFNsyn-coated substrates was also delayed in the first 30 min (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell area quantification data in Figure 2C.

claim: Time-lapse video microscopy reveals delayed cell spreading on pFNsyn and unstable adhesions consisting of several cycles of binding and release from the substrate.
source: Time-lapse video microscopy confirmed the delayed cell spreading on pFNsyn and revealed unstable adhesions consisting of several cycles of binding and release from the substrate (see Video 1, Video 2 and still images in Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by video microscopy data in Video 1, Video 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The synergy site is dispensable for FN fibril formation but promotes the transition from NAs to FAs.
source: These findings indicate that the synergy site is dispensable for FN fibril formation but promotes the transition from NAs to FAs.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the FN assembly and focal adhesion data.

claim: The τ50 values of Fn1-KO cells decreased on purified full-length pFNsyn by 16% compared to pFNwt.
source: Interestingly, the τ50 values of Fn1-KO cells decreased on purified full-length pFNsyn by 16% compared to pFNwt (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is stated in the text with a specific percentage and supported by spinning disk assay data in Figure 3A.

claim: The τ50 values of Fn1-KO cells decreased on FNIII7-10syn fragment by 43% compared to FNIII7-10wt.
source: Interestingly, the τ50 values of Fn1-KO cells decreased on purified full-length pFNsyn by 16% compared to pFNwt (Figure 3A), and by 43% on FNIII7-10syn fragment compared to FNIII7-10wt
evidence: This is stated in the text with a specific percentage and supported by spinning disk assay data in Figure 3A.

claim: Cells develop less adhesion strength on the synergy site-deficient pFN.
source: and by 43% on FNIII7-10syn fragment compared to FNIII7-10wt, indicating that cells develop less adhesion strength on the synergy site-deficient pFN
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the spinning disk assay data showing reduced τ50 values.

claim: Higher adhesion strengths arise on full-length FN compared to FNIII7-10 fragments.
source: and by 43% on FNIII7-10syn fragment compared to FNIII7-10wt, indicating that cells develop less adhesion strength on the synergy site-deficient pFN and that higher adhesion strengths arise on full-length FN compared to FNIII7-10 fragments.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by comparing τ50 values between full-length FN and FNIII7-10 fragments.

claim: The amount of α5 integrins crosslinked to FN in Fn1-KO fibroblasts is reduced to 60% on pFNsyn.
source: We found that the amount of α5 integrins crosslinked to FN in Fn1-KO fibroblasts was reduced to 60% on pFNsyn (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a specific percentage and supported by crosslinking assay data in Figure 3B.

claim: Upon spinning, Fn1-KO cells increase the proportion of α5 integrins crosslinked to pFNwt.
source: Upon spinning, Fn1-KO cells increased the proportion of α5 integrins crosslinked to pFNwt.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by crosslinking assay data showing increased crosslinking after spinning.

claim: In cells on pFNsyn, tension is unable to increase the number of crosslinked bonds upon spinning.
source: Importantly, in cells on pFNsyn, the tension was unable to increase the number of crosslinked bonds upon spinning and their numbers remained at the same levels as before spinning (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by crosslinking assay data in Figure 3B.

claim: Spinning force strengthens α5β1-mediated adhesion to FN in a synergy site-dependent manner.
source: which altogether indicates that the spinning force strengthens α5β1-mediated adhesion to FN in a synergy site-dependent manner.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the crosslinking assay data showing force-dependent bond strengthening only on pFNwt.

claim: pY397-FAK levels are reduced by 54% when cells are plated on pFNsyn compared to pFNwt.
source: Furthermore and in line with a report showing that the conversion of FN-α5β1 bonds from a relaxed to a tensioned state induces phosphorylation of focal adhesion kinase (FAK) on Y397 (Guan et al., 1991; Kornberg et al., 1992), pY397-FAK levels were reduced by 54% when cells were plated on pFNsyn compared to pFNwt (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a specific percentage and supported by Western blot data in Figure 3C, along with citations to prior work.

claim: Phosphorylation of Y861-FAK is indistinguishable in cells seeded on pFNwt or pFNsyn.
source: Importantly, phosphorylation of Y861-FAK, which occurs independent of substrate binding (Shi and Boettiger, 2003), was indistinguishable in cells seeded on pFNwt or pFNsyn (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Western blot data in Figure 3C, along with a citation to prior work.

claim: Fibroblasts attached to pFNsyn perceive insufficient information regarding substrate stiffness.
source: Since the intensity of FAK Y397 phosphorylation was shown to operate as a sensor for ECM rigidity (Seong et al., 2013), we conclude that fibroblasts attached to pFNsyn perceive insufficient information regarding substrate stiffness.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the reduced pY397-FAK levels on pFNsyn, along with a citation to prior work on FAK as a rigidity sensor.

claim: pKO-β1 cells exhibit reduced adhesion on pFNsyn compared to pFNwt at all time points analyzed.
source: From the three cell lines, only pKO-β1 cells exhibited reduced adhesion on pFNsyn compared to pFNwt at all-time points analyzed (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by adhesion assay data in Figure 4A.

claim: pKO-β1 cells have significantly fewer FAs, contain fewer stress fibers, and spread less on pFNsyn compared to pFNwt.
source: Moreover, pKO-β1 cells had significantly fewer FAs, contained fewer stress fibers, and spread less on pFNsyn compared to pFNwt (Figure 4B–F, see Videos 3 and 4 and still images in Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by quantification data in Figure 4B–F and video microscopy data.

claim: The areas of FAs determined with paxillin and β1 integrin stainings are significantly reduced on pFNsyn compared to pFNwt in pKO-β1 cells.
source: Moreover, the areas of FAs determined with paxillin and β1 integrin stainings were significantly reduced on pFNsyn compared to pFNwt (Figure 4G,H)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by quantification data in Figure 4G,H.

claim: pFNsyn-bound α5β1 integrins fail to organize functional adhesion sites and to induce contractile stress fibers required for cell spreading.
source: which altogether suggests that pFNsyn-bound α5β1 integrins fail to organize functional adhesion sites and to induce contractile stress fibers required for cell spreading.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the reduced FA formation and spreading data in pKO-β1 cells on pFNsyn.

claim: pKO-αv cells adhere and spread similarly on pFNwt and pFNsyn.
source: pKO-αv cells adhered and spread similarly on pFNwt and pFNsyn, and developed comparably large, paxillin-positive FAs that were anchored to thick stress fibers (Figure 4B,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4B,D.

claim: pKO-αv/β1 cells show the same adhesion and spreading behavior, and develop similar adhesion sites on pFNsyn, indicating that αv-containing integrins compensate for the absence of a functional synergy site.
source: Importantly, pKO-αv/β1 cells also showed the same adhesion and spreading behavior, and developed similar adhesion sites on pFNsyn indicating that αv-containing integrins compensate for the absence of a functional synergy site (Figure 4B,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4B,E.

claim: On FNIII7-10wt, pKO-αv and pKO-αv/β1 cells show a 3-fold higher binding probability compared to pKO-β1 cells.
source: On FNIII7-10wt, the experiments revealed a 3-fold higher binding probability of pKO-αv and pKO-αv/β1 cells compared to pKO-β1 cells, indicating that αvβ3 integrins have a higher affinity for FN-RGD than α5β1 integrins.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by single-cell force spectroscopy data.

claim: αvβ3 integrins have a higher affinity for FN-RGD than α5β1 integrins.
source: On FNIII7-10wt, the experiments revealed a 3-fold higher binding probability of pKO-αv and pKO-αv/β1 cells compared to pKO-β1 cells, indicating that αvβ3 integrins have a higher affinity for FN-RGD than α5β1 integrins.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the binding probability data from single-cell force spectroscopy.

claim: Full-length pFN shows higher binding probability than fragments for all cell lines tested including the pKO cells that lack integrin expression.
source: Interestingly, however, full-length pFN showed higher binding probability than fragments for all cell lines tested including the pKO cells that lack integrin expression
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by single-cell force spectroscopy data comparing full-length FN to fragments.

claim: In addition to integrins, other FN-binding cell surface receptor(s) contribute to the initial binding.
source: which altogether suggests that in addition to integrins also other FN-binding cell surface receptor(s) contribute to the initial binding.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the observation that integrin-null pKO cells still show binding to full-length FN.

claim: The FN synergy site promotes the maturation of FAs but accelerates neither the rates of FN binding to α5β1 integrins nor the formation of NAs.
source: These findings indicate that the FN synergy site promotes the maturation of FAs but accelerates neither the rates of FN binding to α5β1 integrins nor the formation of NAs.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the single-cell force spectroscopy and focal adhesion data.

claim: Around 87% of Itgb3-null mice are born and around 40% of them survive the first year of life.
source: Itgb3-null mice fail to express the widely expressed αvβ3 integrins and the platelet-specific αIIbβ3 integrin, and suffer from a bleeding disorder resembling human Glanzmann thrombasthenia. Around 87% of Itgb3-null mice are born and around 40% of them survive the first year of life (Hodivala-Dilke et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to prior work (Hodivala-Dilke et al., 1999).

claim: One instead of the expected 38 compound homozygous Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- mice survived to P21 out of 335 offspring.
source: Out of the 335 offspring altogether, one instead of the expected 38 compound homozygous Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- mice survived to P21.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by breeding data in Table 1.

claim: The single surviving Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- mouse died at the age of 5 months from excessive bleeding.
source: The survivor died at the age of 5 months from excessive bleeding.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an observation from the breeding experiments.

claim: Compound homozygous Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos were present at the expected Mendelian distribution until E15.5.
source: While compound homozygous Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos were present at the expected Mendelian distribution until E15.5, no live embryos were present at E16.5 or later.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by embryo genotyping data in Table 1.

claim: No live Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos were present at E16.5 or later.
source: While compound homozygous Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos were present at the expected Mendelian distribution until E15.5, no live embryos were present at E16.5 or later.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by embryo genotyping data in Table 1.

claim: Mice with one wild-type Itgb3 allele (Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/+) were normally distributed.
source: Interestingly, mice with one wild-type Itgb3 allele (Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/+) were normally distributed, which altogether indicates that one β3 integrin allele is sufficient to compensate for normal development.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by breeding data in Table 1.

claim: One β3 integrin allele is sufficient to compensate for normal development in the context of the Fn1syn mutation.
source: Interestingly, mice with one wild-type Itgb3 allele (Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/+) were normally distributed, which altogether indicates that one β3 integrin allele is sufficient to compensate for normal development.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the normal distribution of Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/+ mice.

claim: Compound homozygous Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos display multiple cutaneous hemorrhages and edema, first visible at E11.5/12.5.
source: Compound homozygous Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos displayed multiple cutaneous hemorrhages and edema, which were first visible at E11.5/12.5 (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and then spread over the whole body at E15.5 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by embryo images in Figure 5A, Figure 5B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Lyve1-positive lymphatic vessels in the skin of Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos are dilated and covered with ectopic α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA)-positive cells and filled with Ter119-positive erythroblasts.
source: In line with our hypothesis, Lyve1-positive lymphatic vessels in the skin of Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos were dilated and covered with ectopic α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA)-positive cells and filled with Ter119-positive erythroblasts (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunostaining data in Figure 5C–E.

claim: Lymphatic vessels in the skin of Itgb3-null or wild-type littermates neither contain Ter119-positive cells nor are surrounded with α-smooth muscle actin-positive cells.
source: In contrast, lymphatic vessels in the skin of Itgb3-null or wild-type littermates neither contained Ter119-positive cells nor were surrounded with α-smooth muscle actin-positive cells.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunostaining data showing normal lymphatic vessels in control embryos.

claim: The mean spreading area of wild-type platelets seeded for 60 min on fibrinogen, pFNwt, and pFNsyn is 15–16 μm2.
source: The mean spreading area of wild-type platelets seeded for 60 min on fibrinogen, pFNwt, and pFNsyn was 15–16 μm2.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by platelet spreading assay data.

claim: Itgb3-/- platelets fail to spread on fibrinogen (mean spreading area of 4.6 μm2).
source: As expected, Itgb3-/- platelets failed to spread on fibrinogen (mean spreading area of 4.6 μm2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by platelet spreading assay data.

claim: Itgb3-/- platelets show a reduced mean spreading area of 8.9 μm2 on pFNwt.
source: Furthermore, they showed a reduced mean spreading area of 8.9 μm2 on pFNwt and failed to spread on pFNsyn (mean spreading area of 3.8 μm2) (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by platelet spreading assay data in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Itgb3-/- platelets fail to spread on pFNsyn (mean spreading area of 3.8 μm2).
source: Furthermore, they showed a reduced mean spreading area of 8.9 μm2 on pFNwt and failed to spread on pFNsyn (mean spreading area of 3.8 μm2) (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by platelet spreading assay data in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Application of shear flow reduces adhesion of wild-type platelets to pFNsyn by 10-fold compared to pFNwt.
source: Application of shear flow reduced adhesion of wild-type platelets to pFNsyn by 10-fold compared to pFNwt, while adhesion of Itgb3-null platelets was lost on fibrinogen as well as pFNsyn, and only slightly diminished on pFNwt (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by flow chamber assay data in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Adhesion of Itgb3-null platelets is lost on fibrinogen and pFNsyn under shear flow.
source: Application of shear flow reduced adhesion of wild-type platelets to pFNsyn by 10-fold compared to pFNwt, while adhesion of Itgb3-null platelets was lost on fibrinogen as well as pFNsyn, and only slightly diminished on pFNwt (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by flow chamber assay data in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Adhesion and spreading of platelets isolated from Itgb3-/- mice to collagen are unaffected, irrespective of whether shear flow is applied or not.
source: Importantly, adhesion and spreading of platelets isolated from Itgb3-/- mice to collagen were unaffected, irrespective of whether shear flow was applied or not (Figure 6C,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by platelet adhesion and spreading data on collagen in Figure 6C,E.

claim: Adhesion of αIIbβ3-deficient platelets to wild-type FN is partially compensated by α5β1 integrins in a FN synergy site-dependent manner.
source: These in vitro experiments demonstrate that adhesion of αIIbβ3-deficient platelets to wild-type FN is partially compensated by α5β1 integrins in a FN synergy site-dependent manner
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the platelet adhesion and spreading data comparing Itgb3-/- platelets on pFNwt vs pFNsyn.

claim: α5β1 and αIIbβ3 integrins require the FN synergy site for stabilizing platelet adhesion to FN under shear flow.
source: and that α5β1 as well as αIIbβ3 integrins require the FN synergy site for stabilizing platelet adhesion to FN, under shear flow.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the flow chamber assay data showing reduced platelet adhesion on pFNsyn under shear flow.

claim: The arteries and veins of the dermal vasculature of E15.5 Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos are tortuous and irregularly covered with α-SMA-positive cells.
source: While immunostaining of E11.5 whole mount embryos with an anti-PECAM-1 antibody revealed that the vessels in the trunk of Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos showed normal sprouting (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), the arteries and veins of the dermal vasculature of E15.5 embryos were tortuous and irregularly covered with α-SMA-positive cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunostaining data in Figure 7A.

claim: The vascular network has significantly fewer branching points in Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos compared to wild-type littermates.
source: Furthermore, the vascular network was less intricate and had significantly fewer branching points in Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos compared to wild-type littermates (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by quantification data in Figure 7B.

claim: Many small vessels in E15.5 Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos lack a clear lumen and PECAM-1 immunosignals, representing retracted vessels.
source: Interestingly, collagen IV immunostaining indicated that many small vessels in E15.5 Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos lacked a clear lumen and PECAM-1 immunosignals (see arrowheads in Figure 7C). They probably represent retracted vessels and were significantly more frequent in Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos compared to wild-type, Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3+/+ and Fn1+/+;Itgb3-/- littermates (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunostaining and quantification data in Figure 7C,D.

claim: Small vessels in Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos are often less covered by pericytes, with NG2-positive pericytes either detached or forming patchy aggregates on the vessel surface.
source: Moreover, small vessels in Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos were often less covered by pericytes. Instead, NG2-positive pericytes were either detached or formed patchy aggregates on the vessel surface (see arrowheads in Figure 7E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunostaining data in Figure 7E.

claim: The vessel wall coverage and stability are decreased in the Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos and probably contribute to their severe hemorrhages.
source: Altogether, these observations indicate that the vessel wall coverage and stability are decreased in the Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos and probably contribute to their severe hemorrhages.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the vascular defects observed in Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos.

claim: Ablation of the Fn1 gene in mice arrests development at embryonic day 8.5 (E8.5) due to defects in the formation of mesoderm and mesoderm-derived structures.
source: Ablation of the Fn1 gene in mice, as well as the simultaneous ablations of the Itga5/Itgav integrin genes in mice arrests development at embryonic day 8.5 (E8.5) due to defects in the formation of mesoderm and mesoderm-derived structures (George et al., 1993; Georges-Labouesse et al., 1996; Yang et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work (George et al., 1993; Georges-Labouesse et al., 1996; Yang et al., 1999).

claim: The replacement of the FNIII10 RGD motif with RGE in mice affects mesoderm development, restricted to the vascular system and to the posterior region of the developing embryo.
source: The replacement of the FNIII10 RGD motif with the RGE in mice also affects mesoderm development, although less severe and restricted to the vascular system and to the posterior region of the developing embryo (Takahashi et al., 2007; Girós et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work (Takahashi et al., 2007; Girós et al., 2011).

claim: The RGE mutation is sufficient to abrogate α5β1 integrin function.
source: Interestingly, these defects resemble those observed in Itga5-deficient mice indicating that the RGE mutation is sufficient to abrogate α5β1 integrin function and that the synergy site cannot compensate for a dysfunctional RGD motif.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by comparison to Itga5-deficient mice phenotypes.

claim: The synergy site cannot compensate for a dysfunctional RGD motif.
source: Interestingly, these defects resemble those observed in Itga5-deficient mice indicating that the RGE mutation is sufficient to abrogate α5β1 integrin function and that the synergy site cannot compensate for a dysfunctional RGD motif.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the phenotypic similarity between RGE mutant and Itga5-deficient mice.

claim: The normal development of Fn1syn/syn mice excludes an essential role of the synergy site for α5 integrin function in vivo.
source: Furthermore, the normal development of Fn1syn/syn mice also excludes an essential role of the synergy site for α5 integrin function in vivo (Grant et al., 1997; Krammer et al., 2002).
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the normal development observed in Fn1syn/syn mice, with citations to prior hypotheses.

claim: The absence of obvious 'α5β1-loss-of-function defects' in Fn1syn/syn mice indicates that the synergy site is probably dispensable to accelerate α5β1 integrin-FN binding.
source: However, the absence of obvious 'α5β1-loss-of-function defects' (Yang et al., 1993) in Fn1syn/syn mice and the normal FN-binding on-rates of pKO-β1 cells in single-cell force spectroscopy experiments indicate that the synergy site is probably dispensable to accelerate α5β1 integrin-FN binding.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the normal development of Fn1syn/syn mice and single-cell force spectroscopy data, with a citation to prior work.

claim: There is an unexpected, compensatory role between the FN synergy site and αvβ3 integrins for the vascular coverage by smooth muscle cells.
source: We also demonstrate an unexpected, compensatory role between the FN synergy site and αvβ3 integrins for the vascular coverage by smooth muscle cells.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the severe vascular defects in Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos.

claim: High myosin II-induced forces generated by smooth muscle cells are only efficiently absorbed with either high αv-class integrin surface levels or a fully functional FN.
source: Apparently, the high myosin II-induced forces generated by these cells are only efficiently absorbed with either high αv-class integrin surface levels or a fully functional FN.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the vascular smooth muscle cell defects in Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos.

claim: There is clear evidence for a compensatory role of the FN synergy site and αv-class integrins for cell spreading and FA maturation in vitro.
source: Interestingly, we also find clear evidence for a compensatory role of the FN synergy site and αv-class integrins for cell spreading and FA maturation in vitro (Figure 8)
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the cell-based assays with different integrin-expressing cell lines, with reference to Figure 8.

claim: Platelet adhesion to pFN, mediated by αIIbβ3 with contributions from α5β1 and other integrins, plays a critical role for hemostasis.
source: It is well known that platelet adhesion to pFN, mediated by αIIbβ3 with contributions from α5β1 and other integrins, plays a critical role for hemostasis (Wang et al., 2014; Ni et al., 2003b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work (Wang et al., 2014; Ni et al., 2003b).

claim: The FN synergy site is critically important for the adhesion of wild type platelets in in vitro flow chamber settings.
source: Our findings revealed that the FN synergy site is critically important for the adhesion of wild type platelets in in vitro flow chamber settings, while impaired spreading or defects under static adhesion only arise when αIIbβ3 expression is lost.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the flow chamber assay data with wild-type and Itgb3-/- platelets.

claim: The synergy site plays a central role as soon as force is applied to the bonds between FN and platelet integrins.
source: These findings indicate that the synergy site plays a central role as soon as force is applied to the bonds between FN and platelet integrins.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the differential effects of the synergy site mutation under static vs flow conditions.

claim: The requirement of the synergy site for platelets to resist the shear forces of the blood flow provides a rational explanation for the prolonged bleeding times observed in Fn1syn/syn mice after tail tip excisions.
source: This requirement of the synergy site for platelets to resist the shear forces of the blood flow also provides a rational explanation for the prolonged bleeding times observed in Fn1syn/syn mice after tail tip excisions.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and connects the in vitro flow chamber findings to the in vivo bleeding phenotype.

claim: Murine platelets contain around 100 times more αIIbβ3 than α5β1 integrins.
source: Since murine platelets contain around 100 times more αIIbβ3 than α5β1 integrins (Zeiler et al., 2014) the compensation of the entire αIIbβ3 pool by the minor α5β1-FNwt complexes underscores the fundamental role of the adhesion strengthening property of the synergy site in FN.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior published work (Zeiler et al., 2014).

claim: The compensation of the entire αIIbβ3 pool by the minor α5β1-FNwt complexes underscores the fundamental role of the adhesion strengthening property of the synergy site in FN.
source: Since murine platelets contain around 100 times more αIIbβ3 than α5β1 integrins (Zeiler et al., 2014) the compensation of the entire αIIbβ3 pool by the minor α5β1-FNwt complexes underscores the fundamental role of the adhesion strengthening property of the synergy site in FN.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the text and supported by the platelet adhesion data showing α5β1 can partially compensate for αIIbβ3 loss on wild-type FN.

claim: Adhesion of Fn1-KO cells to pFNwt and pFNsyn begins around 3 min after cell seeding and increases with time without noticeable differences.
source: Adhesion of Fn1-KO cells to pFNwt and pFNsyn began around 3 min after cell seeding and increased with time without noticeable differences (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by adhesion assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The separation of the primary lymphatic sac from the cardinal vein is driven by platelet adhesion to and aggregation at the lymphatic endothelium.
source: The separation of the primary lymphatic sac from the cardinal vein is driven by platelet adhesion to and aggregation at the lymphatic endothelium (Carramolino et al., 2010; Uhrin et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work (Carramolino et al., 2010; Uhrin et al., 2010).

claim: Platelet functions are severely compromised in Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos as they lack αIIbβ3-mediated binding to fibrinogen and FN, as well as the ability to strengthen adhesion and signaling via α5β1 integrin-mediated binding to FN.
source: We therefore hypothesized that the platelet functions are severely compromised in Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos as they lack αIIbβ3-mediated binding to fibrinogen and FN (Figure 6A), as well as the ability to strengthen adhesion and signaling via α5β1 integrin-mediated binding to FN.
evidence: This hypothesis is stated in the text and supported by the platelet adhesion and spreading data, with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: The vessels in the trunk of Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos show normal sprouting at E11.5.
source: While immunostaining of E11.5 whole mount embryos with an anti-PECAM-1 antibody revealed that the vessels in the trunk of Fn1syn/syn;Itgb3-/- embryos showed normal sprouting (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunostaining data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Type I and II modules of FN are stabilized by internal disulfide bonds.
source: FN consists of three different repeating Ig-like folded units, called type I-III modules. Whereas type I and II modules are stabilized by internal disulfide bonds, the 15 type III repeats of FN lack disulfide bonds, which confers elasticity to FN fibrils and the ability to modulate fibril rigidity (Erickson, 1994; Oberhauser et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is based on established scientific knowledge about FN structure, supported by citations (Erickson, 1994; Oberhauser et al., 2002).

claim: The 15 type III repeats of FN lack disulfide bonds, which confers elasticity to FN fibrils and the ability to modulate fibril rigidity.
source: Whereas type I and II modules are stabilized by internal disulfide bonds, the 15 type III repeats of FN lack disulfide bonds, which confers elasticity to FN fibrils and the ability to modulate fibril rigidity (Erickson, 1994; Oberhauser et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is based on established scientific knowledge about FN structure, supported by citations (Erickson, 1994; Oberhauser et al., 2002).

claim: FN is secreted as a disulfide-bonded dimer and assembled into fibrils of variable diameters.
source: FN is secreted as a disulfide-bonded dimer, assembled into fibrils of variable diameters and then crosslinked into a fibrillar network of variable rigidity (Leiss et al., 2008) that binds to and serves as a scaffold for numerous other ECM molecules.
evidence: This statement is based on established scientific knowledge about FN assembly, supported by citation (Leiss et al., 2008).

claim: Soluble plasma (p) FN is required for the stability of blood clots.
source: Soluble plasma (p) FN is required for the stability of blood clots (Ni et al., 2003b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior published work (Ni et al., 2003b).

claim: αIIbβ3 integrins mediate the uptake of pFN into platelet α-granules.
source: Since αIIbβ3 integrins mediate the uptake of pFN into platelet α-granules (Ni et al., 2003a)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior published work (Ni et al., 2003a).

claim: The assembly of FN into a fibrillar network depends on α5β1 binding to FN.
source: The assembly of FN into a fibrillar network depends on α5β1 binding to FN (Fogerty et al., 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior published work (Fogerty et al., 1990).

claim: The conversion of FN-α5β1 bonds from a relaxed to a tensioned state induces phosphorylation of focal adhesion kinase (FAK) on Y397.
source: Furthermore and in line with a report showing that the conversion of FN-α5β1 bonds from a relaxed to a tensioned state induces phosphorylation of focal adhesion kinase (FAK) on Y397 (Guan et al., 1991; Kornberg et al., 1992)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior published work (Guan et al., 1991; Kornberg et al., 1992).

claim: Phosphorylation of Y861-FAK occurs independent of substrate binding.
source: Importantly, phosphorylation of Y861-FAK, which occurs independent of substrate binding (Shi and Boettiger, 2003)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior published work (Shi and Boettiger, 2003).

claim: The intensity of FAK Y397 phosphorylation operates as a sensor for ECM rigidity.
source: Since the intensity of FAK Y397 phosphorylation was shown to operate as a sensor for ECM rigidity (Seong et al., 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior published work (Seong et al., 2013).

claim: Simultaneous engagement of the RGD motif and the synergy site enables α5β1 and αIIbβ3 integrins to induce tensioned bonds.
source: Simultaneous engagement of the RGD motif and the synergy site was suggested to enable α5β1 and αIIbβ3 integrins to induce tensioned bonds, which form when receptor and ligand are in close proximity and hence, can be chemically cross-linked (Shi and Boettiger, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior published work (Shi and Boettiger, 2003).

claim: Itgb3-null mice fail to express the widely expressed αvβ3 integrins and the platelet-specific αIIbβ3 integrin, and suffer from a bleeding disorder resembling human Glanzmann thrombasthenia.
source: Itgb3-null mice fail to express the widely expressed αvβ3 integrins and the platelet-specific αIIbβ3 integrin, and suffer from a bleeding disorder resembling human Glanzmann thrombasthenia.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about the Itgb3-null mouse model.
